Many capable people never even ask for knowledge, he laments. Young English travelers abroad draw his special scorn here. They waste fine chances through incuriosity and ease. His son must instead question, observe, and take pains. This year's letters press industry as the base of every grace. He praises questions as the sign of a living mind. Travel, he insists, rewards only the traveler who looks.
nasa-tm-19630004027-some-aerodynamic-and:
Frank L. Clark and Joanna M. Evans of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-338, in November 1960. It studies craft shapes meant to glide back from space. These lifting reentry shapes were tested at steep angles of attack. Angles ran up to ninety degrees, fully sideways to the wind.

The tests ran at Mach 2.91, near three times sound's speed. The team measured air forces and how well controls worked. A lifting shape could steer its fall and land like a plane. That promise drove much early work on winged spacecraft. Clark and Evans gave designers hard numbers on control at angles no normal plane would ever fly.
nasa-tm-19650019820-effect-on-surface-th:
Herman Mark, Ralph D Sommers, and Michael J Mirtich at Lewis Research Center prepared this paper for a January 1965 meeting in New York. Tiny meteoroid grains strike spacecraft surfaces at great speed. Over time, those hits can change how a surface handles heat. The team reproduced that exposure in a controlled way, using very small fast particles.

A surface that absorbs or sheds heat differently can upset a spacecraft's temperature balance. Calibrated exposure means the test dose is known and measured. The study links that known dose to changes in thermal properties. Designers of long-lived spacecraft needed such data to predict how surfaces age in orbit.
nasa-tm-19650022587-low-temperature-mech:
W R Morgan, at Marshall Space Flight Center, measured how a strong steel alloy sheet behaves in deep cold for this July 23, 1965, report. The alloy is HP 9-4-25, a nickel-cobalt martensitic steel. Sheet about a sixteenth of an inch thick was tested from room heat down to the cold of liquid hydrogen temperatures.

Morgan found that both ultimate tensile strength and yield strength were considerably greater at the cold end. Cold can also make some metals brittle, so full data matter. Rocket tanks and lines hold fuels at such extreme cold. Designers need measured properties, not guesses, for the metals that contain them.
nasa-tm-19660012403-transonic-aerodynami:
Edward J Ray and Robert T Taylor at Langley tested a model supersonic airliner with no tail in a wind tunnel, for this March 1966 report. Speeds were transonic, around the speed of sound. The model had a fixed wing, rather than a swing wing. A tailless layout cuts weight and drag, but it must still stay stable and controllable at low speed.

The pair report the model's aerodynamic characteristics through that tricky speed range. Supersonic transports were a major design goal of the era. Tunnel data on bold layouts like this one showed which ideas deserved more work. Ray and Taylor give the measured base for judging the tailless transport concept.
nasa-tm-19660016087-a-calculation-method:
John D Warmbrod, in Marshall's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory, presented a full calculation method in this April 12, 1966, report for blunt bodies tipped with glass. On entry into an atmosphere, a blunt body's nose heats fiercely. A glass tip melts and flows away, carrying heat with it. That wearing away is called ablation. Warmbrod's method computes the flight path and the ablation at the nose point.

Both results are needed together, since the path sets the heating and the heating sets the loss. His method is given in detail for other engineers to use. Glass-tipped shapes were studied for entry vehicles that must survive a short, brutal heating pulse.
nasa-tm-19660020011-apollo-spacecraft-bp:
Kennedy Space Center's planning and technical support staff compiled this day-by-day record of Apollo spacecraft BP-15. BP-15 was a boilerplate spacecraft, a full-weight stand-in used for ground tests. The chronology runs from the arrival of its service module and adapter through the postlaunch report, per the catalog note. Each step of technical progress at the center is entered in order.

Chronologies preserve who did what, and when, in a huge program. Later questions about a test or a fault can be answered from such a record. Boilerplate flights tested launch and recovery steps without risking a flight-ready craft. The BP-15 record shows Kennedy Space Center learning its Apollo work piece by piece.
nasa-tm-19660030642-a-preface-to-the-non:
A. Temkin, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, offers this July 1966 paper as a preface, a set of first steps. Its subject is what happens when an electron strikes a hydrogen atom hard enough to knock another electron free. That process is called ionization, and Temkin treats it with nonadiabatic theory.

He gives preliminary considerations and solves a simpler first version of the problem. That solution points to a threshold law for how ionization starts. His results show a strong suppression of cases where the two outgoing electrons share energy equally. Extending the results deepens that suppression near equal energies, setting up the fuller theory to come.
nasa-tm-19670009329-kirchhoff-s-theorem-:
L. A. Chernov wrote this acoustics paper in Russian, published in 1950 in the proceedings of the acoustics commission of the Soviet Academy of Sciences. The English translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in January 1967. It extends Kirchhoff's theorem, a workhorse result in acoustics and optics, to sound traveling through a moving medium.

An earlier generalization by Blokhintsev covered only a uniform flow. Chernov pushes the theorem further, to a medium in potential motion, a broader class of flows. He starts from the refined wave equation for such motion credited to Andreyev and Blokhintsev. After proving an auxiliary lemma, he shows the theorem at work on a concrete problem: a point source of sound sitting inside the flow.
nasa-tm-19670009414-numerical-techniques:
Theodore Katsanis wrote this work as a thesis at the Case Institute of Technology in June 1967. His advisor was Professor Milton Lees. The subject is a class of math problems called symmetric positive linear differential equations. Such equations turn up often in engineering work.

Katsanis develops a finite difference method for solving them. A finite difference method replaces smooth change with small steps a computer can handle. He builds the method to suit the special structure of these equations. The thesis gives later engineers a worked-out recipe for this family of problems.
nasa-tm-19670022198-full-scale-flight-te:
Willard S. Blanchard Jr. and James L. Raper, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, wrote this memorandum in October 1960. It reports a full-scale free flight test, launched from sea level, of the abort-escape system for a Project Mercury capsule. The system existed to pull a crewed capsule to safety if its booster failed at or just after takeoff.

The test article matched the real capsule and escape system at full size. An escape tower with its rocket motor sat atop the capsule, and a small drogue parachute deployed the large landing parachute. The escape system performed satisfactorily, the authors report, reaching a maximum altitude of 1,950 feet. The main parachute gave a steady sinking rate of about twenty-eight feet per second. Accelerations stayed within the tolerance of a properly positioned and supported human. Noise inside the uninsulated capsule peaked near 144 decibels during motor thrust.
nasa-tm-19670022199-design-and-experimen:
Robert R. Nunamaker, Donald A. Petrash, and Charles A. Wasserbauer, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tested turbine blade changes in this investigation. The turbine is a high-weight-flow, low-pressure-ratio, single-stage machine. It was meant for a turbojet engine designed to cruise at four times the speed of sound.

The original rotor blades were thin, tall, and slightly tapered, which raised mechanical worries. One fix pinned neighboring blades together near the tips for support. That version ran below its design efficiency and missed the design flow. The second fix redesigned the blade for strength, and it cost essentially nothing in performance.
nasa-tm-19670026973-an-analysis-of-the-m:
James O. Ballance, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this analysis on July 31, 1967. It examines the molecular kinetics of the thermosphere probe. That probe measured gas temperature and density high in the atmosphere, where air is so thin that molecules rarely collide.

Ballance ran a Monte Carlo computer analysis of the free molecular flow. He calculated the transmission probability that links the outside density to the measured density. His simplified model matched measured signals well, except at high angles of attack. The results also suggested incoming molecules bounced at most once, if at all.
nasa-tm-19670028445-the-use-of-dsl-90-fo:
R. A. Lewallen and H. H. Trauboth, of the Computation Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on June 28, 1967. It tests a digital simulation language called DSL/90. Their test problem is the dynamics of a stabilized platform, the gimbaled base that keeps guidance instruments steady.

The authors set out to get a feel for the power of the language. The catalog record specifies the application: simulation of the Saturn guidance system's stabilized platform. A guidance platform must hold its orientation while the rocket moves around it. Showing that DSL/90 could model such motion proved the language on a real engineering problem.
nasa-tm-19680001615-effect-of-axial-flow:
Howard A. Stine, Velvin R. Watson, and Charles E. Shepard, of Ames Research Center in California, studied an electric arc blown by its own gas stream. They presented the work in Belgium in September 1964. The arc is wall-constricted, held narrow by the tube around it, with gas flowing along its axis.

Their study mixes experiment with theory. It covers sizes and pressures where radiation carries off a noticeable share of the energy. New numerical calculations are compared with older analytic ones and with the measurements. The two theories differ in detailed behavior, they find. Yet both give essentially the same overall picture, matching the experiments.
nasa-tm-19680012471-aerodynamic-characte:
Odell A. Morris and Milton Lamb, at the Langley Research Center in Virginia, compared two odd supersonic shapes in the unitary plan wind tunnel. One model wore a half-ring wing; the other, a swept wing. Both sat on the same kind of wide, flat body, with swappable nose and tail sections.

Tests ran from Mach 2.16 to Mach 3.70, measuring pitch behavior. Both shapes gained favorable extra lift from interference at zero angle of attack. The ring wing gained the most. Yet the swept wing won the best lift-to-drag scores, because its lift grew faster with angle. Changing nose and tail shapes made no real difference to those best scores.
nasa-tm-19680013884-capillary-rise-in-th:
Raymond F. Lacovic and James A. Berns of the Lewis Research Center wrote this May 1968 NASA memorandum, numbered TM X-1558. Their subject is capillary rise, the pull that draws liquid up a narrow gap, in the ring-shaped space between two concentric cylinders. The case they study is the fuel sensing gear aboard Atlas-Centaur rockets during quiet coast periods.

Flight data from three Atlas-Centaur missions gave the rise height over time at very low gravity levels. The longest coast lasted well over twenty minutes, far beyond earlier drop tower tests. The authors matched the flight data with a math formula that, in their words, accurately described the flow. Their work extended capillary studies to cold rocket fuels such as liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.
nasa-tm-19680023734-the-latitudinal-temp:
H. G. Mayr, L. H. Brace, and W. Crevier of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this June 1968 report, X-621-68-233. Their subject is the topside ionosphere, the upper part of the charged layer high above Earth. They ask how its electron temperature changes from the equator toward the poles, and whether theory can match satellite readings.

Solving the energy and flow equations for two ion types reproduced the observed pattern up to sixty degrees of latitude. The match showed a cool trough at the equator and warm peaks at middle latitudes. Beyond sixty degrees the theory ran too cold. The authors suggest missing light ions there slow electron cooling, which would lift the real temperature.
nasa-tm-19690013568-an-investigation-of-:
Roger K. Crouch and Gerald D. Walberg of Langley Research Center investigated Avcoat 5026-39/M in this April 1969 memorandum, TM X-1778. Avcoat forms the reentry heat shield of the Apollo command module. The glass-filled plastic chars and wears away in a controlled fashion, carrying heat off with it. The pair tested it far beyond normal Apollo conditions.

Three high-enthalpy wind tunnels at Langley supplied a wide range of pressures, heating, and oxygen flows. Behavior depended strongly on the heat-transfer level, the summary states. At low levels the char wore back about as diffusion theory predicted. At high levels the wear rate climbed fast, and severe mechanical char failure appeared. Oxygen shaped the char only under the gentler conditions.
nasa-tm-19690014407-a-study-from-kinemat:
James B. Eades and George H. Wyatt of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this March 1969 preprint, X-643-69-106, on the kinematics of intercept and pursuit. Kinematics studies motion itself, apart from the forces behind it. Their problems are flat, two-dimensional ones: how should one moving vehicle steer to reach another?

The pair treat the questions from both mathematical and physical viewpoints, with worked examples throughout. Cases include the simple straight-line intercept and pursuit of a target on a straight path. A harder case has the target flying a circular path. Alongside each path they give flight time, range history, and the acceleration the chasing vehicle must endure. Ample graphs picture what happens during each maneuver.
nasa-tm-19690029468-an-experimental-and-:
Billy Grant McKinney of Marshall Space Flight Center studied water heat pipes for moderate temperature ranges in this report, TM X-53849. Heat pipes move heat with no moving parts, suiting spacecraft thermal control well. His working range ran from about two hundred to three hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit, tested in steady operation.

Sixteen pipes were investigated near the vertical: eight as radiating fins, eight with an insulated section and condenser. Instruments recorded heat inputs, surface and interior temperatures, and pressures throughout. Governing equations were programmed so permeability, contact angle, and section length effects could be studied. McKinney also gives screen wick permeability results and an assembly method that keeps the vapor space clean.
nasa-tm-19700025395-apollo-mission-f-per:
Rendezvous charts for Mission F get a performance analysis in this Houston internal note, dated April 29, 1969. Mission F was Apollo 10, the last full rehearsal before the first landing. The charts guided the lunar module's meeting with the command module in lunar orbit after its descent rehearsal.

The analysis sets out its study rules, the digital program used, and the charts themselves. Starting conditions come next, along with errors allowed in sensors and in how burns were carried out. Braking schedules and line-of-sight rate limits round out the setup. Results then report maneuver values, miss distance, fuel used in small correction burns, and arrival timing.
nasa-tm-19700026532-the-concept-of-gener:
Henry P. Decell Jr. wrote this mathematics paper on the generalized inversion of complex matrices. Some matrices have no normal inverse, yet a generalized inverse can still serve in their place. The concept matters wherever large sets of equations must be solved by computer, including the orbit work of its day.

Decell opens by fixing notation for inverses, transposes, and range spaces, then states his aim plainly. The paper investigates how to invert matrices that are singular or not even square. It gives a new algorithm for computing the generalized inverse of any complex matrix. For a matrix that does have an ordinary inverse, the algorithm simply returns that inverse.
nasa-tm-19710013146-subsonic-aerodynamic:
William P Henderson of the Langley Research Center studied a highly swept fixed wing shape at low speed. Tests ran in the Langley high speed seven by ten foot tunnel. The team varied the wing dihedral angle, the upward tilt of the wings. They also changed vertical tails, tail cant, and leading edge flap settings.

Runs covered a Mach number of 0.168 and a wide range of attack angles. Adding the vertical tails improved the static stability of the shape. Instability then held off until a higher lift level. Data of this kind helped designers judge swept wing layouts. Such wings were central to planned fast aircraft of the period.
nasa-tm-19710016707-low-speed-aerodynami:
Anthony M. Cook and Thomas N. Aiken of the Ames Research Center issued this memorandum in March 1971, as NASA TM X-62,017. It reports low-speed wind tunnel tests of a large model of a STOL transport, an aircraft built for short takeoffs and landings. The model carried an augmented jet flap, which boosts lift by blowing engine air through the wing flap.

The tests used configurations picked earlier for landing approach and takeoff, aimed at a proposed flight research aircraft based on the CV-7A Buffalo. The team varied the thrust of the underwing engines and its direction, and measured fuselage boundary-layer control effects. Several lateral control methods were also tried to measure roll control power. Runs were made with and without the horizontal tail in the Ames forty-by-eighty-foot wind tunnel.
nasa-tm-19720016361-large-scale-wind-tun:
Michael D Falarski of the Ames Research Center and the Army Air Mobility laboratory reported this large tunnel study in May 1972, as NASA TM X-62,154. The report runs to one hundred eighteen pages. Its model was half of a wing, over fourteen feet across. A ducted fan blew air over its flap for lift. Such externally blown flaps promised short takeoffs, but they were loud. Falarski measured the noise in detail.

The fan measured thirty inches across and ran at gentle pressure. Flap size changed between test series. The fan's height above the wing also varied. Each change's effect on the sound was recorded. Big models give noise data close to real aircraft scale. The results served the quiet short haul transport effort.
nasa-tm-19720025115-aerodynamic-and-acou:
Brent A. Miller and John M. Abbott wrote this NASA memorandum at the Lewis Research Center in September 1972. They tested two engine inlets, the openings that guide air into a jet fan. Both inlets could choke, or narrow, the flow of air passing through them.

One inlet choked flow by sliding its center body along its axis. The other used a moving grid of small airfoils. The pair ran choked and open, across a range of air flows. Miller and Abbott measured pressure, flow quality, and fan noise. Choking cut fan blade noise by a large margin. Such work pointed toward quieter jet engines.
new-ideas-in-india-during-the-nineteenth:
John Morrison, late principal of the General Assembly's Institution in Calcutta, published New Ideas in India in London in 1907. Macmillan issued the book in London and New York. Morrison had also sat in the senate of Calcutta University. The work began under a lectureship at Edinburgh on science, philosophy, and kindred study.

Chapters open with the new era and Indian conservatism, then new social ideas. One asks what chief thing dissolved the old ideas, and another treats woman's place. Political chapters cover a uniting India and false patriotism. Religious chapters ask if new ideas exist there, then survey Indian Christians, Brahmas, Aryas, and Theosophists.
on-the-spanish-main-or-some-english-fora:
John Masefield published this sea history in London in 1906. Methuen issued the book with twenty-two pictures and a map. Masefield dedicates it to artist Jack B. Yeats. Chapter one tells Drake's voyage to the West Indies. Drake's quarrel with the Spaniards opens the story.

The subtitle promises English forays on the Isthmus of Darien. Masefield also describes the buccaneers who raided there. Old-time ships and sailors receive a short account. Captain William Dampier fronts the book in a portrait. Masefield writes history with a poet's love of the sea. The book suits readers of pirate and exploration tales.
pennsylvania-pilgrim-and-other-poems-par:
John Greenleaf Whittier's narrative poem The Pennsylvania Pilgrim tells of the German Pietists who settled near Philadelphia. An introductory note explains that German emigration to America began with William Penn's 1677 visit to the Continent. There he met the circle of mystics gathered around the pastor Spener.

That circle formed the Frankfort Land Company, which bought Pennsylvania land from Penn. Its agent was Francis Daniel Pastorius, the young lawyer who led the settlers. This part of Whittier's works pairs the long title poem with shorter narrative pieces such as King Volmer and Elsie and The Witch of Wenham.
personal-narrative-of-travels-to-the-equ: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of volume 2 of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, the Bohn's Scientific Library title pages, with no travel text visible. The title page names Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland. It gives their travels to the equinoctial regions of America during 1799 to 1804, translated from the French and edited by Thomasina Ross. This London edition of George Bell and Sons is dated 1907, and notes on local measures, the tablon and the torta, follow the title pages.
religious-poems-part-1-part-5-from-volum:
John Greenleaf Whittier's religious poems are gathered in this part of his works, under a contents list of nearly thirty titles. The Star of Bethlehem leads, followed by The Cities of the Plain and The Call of the Christian. Poems on the Crucifixion, Palestine, and Ezekiel stand among hymns from the French of Lamartine.

Later titles turn inward: My Soul and I, Worship, Trust, and Questions of Life. Andrew Rykman's Prayer and The Cry of a Lost Soul give voices to single speakers. Whittier's Quaker faith speaks in plain verse here, in poems of trust, patience, and prayer drawn from his second volume.
religious-poems-part-2-part-6-from-volum:
A second gathering of John Greenleaf Whittier's religious poems opens with The Answer and The Eternal Goodness, two of his best-known pieces. The Common Question and Our Master follow, then The Meeting and The Clear Vision. Divine Compassion and The Prayer-Seeker keep the inward tone of the set.

Among later titles are The Brewing of Soma, The Prayer of Agassiz, and a Christmas Carmen. Hymn of the Dunkers, The Vision of Echard, and The Friend's Burial reflect Whittier's Quaker world. Short inscriptions for a sun-dial and a fountain, with pieces named Help, Utterance, and Conduct, close a list drawn from his works' second volume.
rembrandt-a-collection-of-fifteen-pictur:
Estelle M. Hurll edited this album of Rembrandt's work for the Masterpieces of Art series, issued by Houghton Mifflin in 1899. It holds fifteen pictures and a portrait of the painter, with her introduction and interpretation. Rembrandt's self-portrait from the National Gallery, London, serves as frontispiece, from a photograph by Maison Ad. Braun.

Her opening parts treat Rembrandt's character as an artist and list books of reference on him. A historical directory of the pictures in the collection follows, with dates and owners. An outline table of the chief events in Rembrandt's life completes the front matter, before the plates and her readings of them.
richard-van-der-borght-the-facts-in-the-: Pages of a scanner's front matter, printed first in English and then in German, are all that open this record. They explain that the book was long kept on library shelves, that its copyright has expired, and that readers must keep their use lawful. No title page of the work itself follows in the pages at hand. Neither its author, its subject, nor any line of its text is shown. Nothing about its case can be reported from these pages.
seven-wives-and-seven-prisons-or-experie:
L. A. Abbott wrote his own life story and published it in New York in 1870, calling himself a matrimonial maniac in the subtitle. Chapter heads promise a first and worst wife, a forgery trial, arrest for bigamy, and a stunning sentence at Northampton. Prison, pardon, and fresh marriages follow in turn.

Abbott learned the brush trade inside state prison, won the warden's friendship, and gained a full pardon. Later chapters chase Sarah Scheimer through plots, pursuits, and midnight rides. Readers get a raw, self-serving memoir of crime and marriage that sold on shock in its day.
shakespeare-s-insomnia-and-the-causes-th:
Franklin H. Head published this piece in 1887, and a transcriber's note warns flatly that it is a literary hoax with made-up letters. The essay opens on sleeplessness as the growing dread of busy men past thirty-five. Youth courts darkness gladly, Head writes, while age finds it full of cares.

Long wakeful stretches parade a man's troubles before him in grim order, Head argues, until morning finds him more worn than night did. The hoax then lays this curse at Shakespeare's door through forged proof. Readers get both a sharp sketch of insomnia and a period joke at scholars' expense.
sketches-and-tales-illustrative-of-life-:
Mrs. F. Beavan published these sketches of backwoods life in New Brunswick in 1845, drawn from seven years of living in that colony. Contents open with who settled the colony and the state of morals and religion there. Spring freshets, cranberries, and stream driving follow in the year's rough order.

Sugar making, the breaking of ice, house moving, and frolics fill later heads. Log huts, a deserted lot, the postman, and mosquitoes all get their due. Beavan writes for old-world readers curious how settlers truly lived, in plain tales gleaned from watching and doing the work herself.
stray-pearls-memoirs-of-margaret-de-riba:
Charlotte Yonge's Stray Pearls takes the form of memoirs of Margaret de Ribaumont, Viscountess of Bellaise, set in the France of the Fronde. In her preface Yonge confesses the construction is faulty. The state of French society beguiled her into the tale. The strange scenes of the Fronde did the rest. The book became a family record rather than a novel.

Yonge explains that the historical romance writer, once free to bend time and bend facts, must now serve as the meek handmaid of history, coloring only the outlines the record leaves undefined. So her heroes and heroines often stand as onlookers while real events drive the catastrophe, spread over a long span of years.
the-adventures-of-col-daniel-boon-contai:
John Filson wrote The Adventures of Col. Daniel Boon, a narrative of the wars of Kentucky drawn from his Discovery and Settlement of Kentucke. Filson opens with a broad claim about man's love of new and striking things.

He marvels that Kentucky, so lately a wild land of woods and beasts, has so fast become a fruitful, settled field. That change came, he notes, in the midst of a raging war and far from the older towns of the coast. Where war cries and groans once sounded, he now hears praise sung in peace. Readers get the first famed life of Daniel Boon, the tale that fixed the hunter's name in American lore.
the-age-of-erasmus-lectures-delivered-in: P. S. Allen, a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, wrote The Age of Erasmus as lectures given at the universities of Oxford and London, printed at the Clarendon Press in 1914. Lectures listed cover the Adwert Academy, schools, monasteries, universities, Erasmus' life-work, force and fraud, private life and manners, pilgrimages, and the transalpine Renaissance.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-01-no-07-may:
American Antiquity leads the May 1858 Atlantic Monthly. Its writer finds the last ten or fifteen years of digging into the past a humbling blow to any proud student of history. Men thought they knew the roots of human events, he says, from Herodotus, Gibbon, and Rollin.

Comfortable fixed points once anchored the deep past: Romulus and Remus, the Phoenicians handing on the alphabet, the fall of Babylon, the date of the Flood. Prescott's works restored the buried empires of America and led readers back through a few plain centuries. Beyond those stations, the writer warns, lies a shadowy land of shifting mists.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-08-jun: Volume two of The Atlantic Monthly begins with its June 1858 number, present here only as an alphabetical contents index. The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table takes three entries, including a visit to the Autocrat and his landlady. Other heads name the American Tract Society, Ann Potter's lesson, Asirvadam the Brahmin, birds of garden, orchard, pasture, and forest, bulls and bears, and a bundle of Irish pennants. The catacombs of Rome, Crawford and sculpture, farming life in New England, Doctor Faustus, and the Illinois in springtime also appear.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-09-jul:
July 1858 closes the Atlantic's account of the catacombs of Rome. The city, the writer says, is above all one of monuments and inscriptions, and the lapidary style, writing on stone, is her most familiar tongue. Republic, Empire, Papacy, heathens, and Christians have all left their record on marble.

Yet gravestones make dull reading, he admits, and inscriptions can run as cold as the stone that holds them. In the Vatican gallery on the way to the library, heathen stones line one side and Christian stones from the catacombs the other. The contrast shows even in outward marks: the old Roman lines are cut with a precision the Christian ones lack.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-19-may:
The May 1859 Atlantic leads with The Gymnasium, a look back at how Greek boys were raised. Two branches of study, joined yet distinct, claimed their early years: music and gymnastics. Plato, the essay notes, put all schooling under those two heads, one for the body and one for the mind.

Grammar sometimes stood apart from music, covering language and something of poetry, speech, and history. Music took in all the arts and sciences under the Muses. Athens knew no separate learned callings as modern times do, and a man's learning ran more mixed. Yet some arts, the essay grants, rose there to a height never since matched, building and sculpture above all.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-03-no-20-jun:
Shakspeare's Art leads the June 1859 number, headed by Ben Jonson's lines that Nature gave the poet his matter while art gave it fashion. Whoever would learn to think in a natural, clear, and logical way, the essay urges, should give days and nights to William Shakspeare.

Such study tunes the ear to phrases whose only habit is fullness of thought and directness of speech. It guards a writer against smooth streams of stock phrases, the essay warns, where a page says weakly what a few firm periods could say with force. These are fresh grounds, it admits, for praising the man long revered as the great poet of Nature.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-21-jul:
July 1859 opens with Thomas Paine's second appearance in the United States. It also carries a warning. Mild modern readers can hardly grasp how bitter party feeling ran in the young republic's early years. A Mississippi congressman hearing a free-soil speech seems gentle beside his grandfathers in office sixty years before.

The same temper ruled the whole land, the essay says. Nobody stood aloof; two hostile camps faced each other, and every man was in his tent. The great experiment was new, and each citizen's own welfare hung on its success. So each man anxiously trained it up the way his reason or his feeling told him promised the best result.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-31-may:
Instinct leads the May 1860 Atlantic, and Falstaff leads the essay. Called to find a hiding trick after running from a fight and hacking his own sword, Falstaff declared that instinct is a great matter. He had run, he claimed, as a lion will not turn on the true prince.

His case was a poor one for calm thought, the writer admits, but his claim was right, and his authority may stand even on a question of the science of mind. That endowment of animals called instinct has filled every age with wonder. Thinkers have long puzzled over how beasts know, without learning, what they most need to do.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-05-no-32-jun:
June 1860 takes up the future of American railways, a subject the writer says should interest everyone. Railways, it has become a common remark, have benefited everybody but their projectors. Many sharp people doubt whether any railway has truly paid a return on the money sunk in it.

One of two ends seems sure: either traffic falls short of paying a dividend, or early profits prove false. Within a few years the road itself wears out so fast that renewal eats more than the earnings, and the gap is filled with new capital or fresh debt. The Illinois Central is pointed out as a case in point.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-33-jul:
July 1860 offers a glance at the science of weather. Its purpose is to set out the chief rules on which that science rests. The writer offers them in brief and simple form. He writes in the spirit of a fellow seeker rather than a teacher.

For all its rapid growth in thirty years, the study is far from an exact science. Many of its sights cannot yet be explained, and learned men still differ on points that look easy. The field has burst its old bounds: vapor and air are a faint hint of its range. It now stands among the leading sciences, tied to heat, light, currents of air, water, plant life, and climate itself.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-43-may:
Agnes of Sorrento, a novel in progress, opens its first chapter in the May 1861 Atlantic. Setting sunbeams slant over the old gateway of Sorrento, fusing into golden bronze the brown stone dress of Saint Antonio. With heavy stone mitre and raised hands, the saint has kept watch there for centuries.

He has a quiet time of it in the golden Italian air, fixed in the act of blessing. Orange lichens and green mosses embroider patterns on the seams of his robes year by year, grass tufts sprout in his folds, and hardy blossoms shower from his wide sleeve-cuffs. Small birds perch on the tip of his nose and the point of his mitre, wiping their beaks, while the world below goes on its way.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-07-no-44-jun:
Chapter five of Agnes of Sorrento, the running novel, leads the June 1861 Atlantic under the head Il Padre Francesco. At the first streak of dawn Elsie wakes, as is her custom, in a bristling state of caution. A hen who has seen a hawk over her chicks could not wake more alarmed.

Spirits in the gorge, indeed, she mutters: spirits in good sound bodies, and next will come rope-ladders and climbings. She vows to go to confession that very morning and tell Father Francesco of the danger. Rather than take the girl down to sell oranges, she will send her to the sisters with a ring and a basket of oranges instead.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-45-jul:
July 1861 opens with a wartime poem, Our Orders, printed in full at the head of the number. Lyons looms are told to weave no more silks to deck girls for gay delights. The crimson flower of battle blooms, and solemn marches fill the nights.

Weave instead, the poem orders, the flag that droops over the early dead. Coarse gray cloth for orphans who must earn their bread is its other demand. Trumpets replace sweet viols, and all the arts are bound in one stern knot while courage draws the lot of mankind. Chapter seven of Agnes of Sorrento, The Day at the Convent, follows the poem.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-55-may:
Man Under Sealed Orders leads the May 1862 Atlantic with a sea picture. A warship leaves port with nobody aboard knowing its errand or its goal. It is a secret government venture, and its commander carries a set of carefully sealed papers holding all his instructions.

Far from his sovereign, those papers are his only authority, the lights on the deep by which he must steer. They provide for every stage: ports to seek and ports to shun, acts for each sea and each chance. Each paper forbids opening the next until its own orders are done, so no one can see past the point he is making for.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-09-no-56-jun:
Walking leads the June 1862 Atlantic, and its writer wishes to speak a word for Nature, for outright freedom and wildness, against a freedom that is merely civil. He would treat man as an inhabitant and parcel of Nature rather than a member of society.

He makes an extreme statement on purpose, since civilization has champions enough: the minister, the school committee, and every reader. Few men, he says, have understood the art of walking, of sauntering. The word comes, he explains, from idle folk of the Middle Ages. They roved the country begging, under pretense of going to the Holy Land. Children cried that there went a Sainte-Terrer, a Holy-Lander.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-57-jul:
Some Soldier-Poetry leads the July 1862 Atlantic. Since Homer's time, the essay holds, the deeds and chances of war have not been happily sung. Where ideas drove the strife, they seldom show to advantage in the poems that record it or praise its heroes.

Set aside the Iliad and the Nibelungenlied. Set aside some English, Spanish, and Northern ballads. Add a few Old Bohemian pieces, Ziska's war-songs, and one or two Romaic. What gleaning of battle poetry is left, the writer says, is startlingly scant. Many of those, too, are more history or myth than true pictures of war. Political songs, by contrast, crowd every country's shelves.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-11-no-67-may:
Charles Lamb's Uncollected Writings leads the May 1863 Atlantic. What Southey says of Cottle's shop, the writer begins, is true of a little bookstore in an old New England town he haunted years ago. There he first peeped into Chaucer, Spenser, Fuller, and Sir Thomas Browne.

Lovers of good books met in that shop to discourse warmly on the merits of their favorite authors. The writer, then a young man hungry for books that are books yet lamentably ignorant of even the chief English names, listened gladly and learned much. He compares the talk to the old Inspector in Hawthorne's Scarlet Letter introduction, holding forth on fish, poultry, and butcher's meat.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-69-jul: Volume twelve of The Atlantic Monthly, dated 1863 in Roman numerals, is present only as a contents index keyed to issue numbers. For issue 69 it names The Claims to Service or Labor by Robert Dale Owen. It names The Growth of Continents by Professor Louis Agassiz. It also names Doings of the Sunbeam by O. W. Holmes. Later issues add Louisa M. Alcott's The Brothers and Debby's Début. They add Hawthorne's Civic Banquets and Sumner on Burke manuscripts. Edward L. Pierce writes on the freedmen at Port Royal.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-13-no-79-may:
A letter describing a steam trip across Lake Ladoga leads the May 1864 Atlantic. The writer tips a friend to a boat, the Valamo, leaving Tuesday the 26th for Serdopol, at the lake's far head. The fare for the round trip is nine rubles, with a return to St. Petersburg promised by six on Saturday evening.

Stoppages on the way include Schlüsselburg, Konewitz Island, Kexholm, and the island monastery of Valaam. There the feast of Saints Sergius and Herrmann falls on Thursday, followed a day later by the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Fine weather may add a run to the Holy Island. Food, the letter warns, can be got on board, but beds probably cannot.
the-botanic-garden-a-poem-in-two-parts-p:
The Botanic Garden is a poem in two parts, with notes on the thought behind the verse. Part I is The Economy of Vegetation and Part II is The Loves of the Plants. A front plate shows Flora dressed by the elements. No author's name is printed on the pages shown.

A short first word states the aim in plain terms. The sheets mean to enlist fancy under the flag of science. They would lead readers from the loose likeness of verse to the strict thought of sound learning. Their true aim is to draw keen minds to botany, by way of the works of Linnaeus, the famed Swede. In the first poem, plant life and the work of the elements on growth are set out. In the second, the sex system of Linnaeus is shown, with the odd traits of many plants.
the-bridal-of-pennacook-part-2-from-volu:
The Bridal of Pennacook stands among the Narrative and Legendary Poems of John Greenleaf Whittier. Its eight parts are The Merrimac, The Bashaba, The Daughter, and The Wedding. The New Home, At Pennacook, The Departure, and Song of Indian Women close the set. A head note in prose tells the tale behind the verse.

Winnepurkit, called George, Sachem of Saugus, wed a daughter of Passaconaway, the great Pennacook chief, in 1662. The wedding took place at Pennacook, now Concord, New Hampshire, and closed with a great feast. Later the wife went home to visit her father, with a brave escort. When she wished to return, each chief held that the other must send her back in the style of a chief. Passaconaway refused, and the tie ended, as Morton's New Canaan is cited to show.
the-care-and-feeding-of-children-a-catec: The Care and Feeding of Children, by L. Emmett Holt, is a catechism for the use of mothers and children's nurses, here in a fourth edition, revised and enlarged. Appleton published it at New York and London in 1907. Its copyrights reach back to 1894. The contents, which a transcriber's note says were added because the scans had none, begin with the care of children: bathing, eyes, mouth, skin, clothing, napkins, and the nursery.
the-church-and-the-empire-being-an-outli: A volume in The Church Universal series, edited by the Rev. W. H. Hutton of St. John's College, Oxford, treats the church and the empire as the fourth of eight brief histories of the church's life. Only the series list and review extracts are present here, praising the first volume, on the church of the apostles, by the Rev. Lonsdale Ragg. No chapter text from this volume follows, and its own author is not named in what is given, so its account cannot be summed up.
the-clockmaker-or-the-sayings-and-doings:
Thomas Chandler Haliburton of Halifax, Nova Scotia, created Samuel Slick of Slickville, the Yankee clockmaker whose sayings fill these sketches. The title page is dated Halifax, 1836, with a Horace motto and a couplet about hiding moral counsel in a tale. An advertisement explains how the sketches reached book form.

The first twenty-one numbers, readers learn, ran in the Novascotian newspaper and grew so popular that its editor asked for the rest. The author agreed, and the whole series appeared together in December 1836. The contents mix letters and talks: the trotting horse, the clockmaker himself, silent girls, Justice Pettifog, and talks at the River Philip. Later pieces treat Yankee eating and horse feeding, the American eagle, and Cumberland oysters. Haliburton uses Slick's shrewd talk to satirize both Yankee push and colonial ease.
the-conditions-of-existence-as-affecting:
Thomas H. Huxley gave this lecture to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863, as the fifth of six lectures on Darwin's Origin of Species. Its subject is the conditions of existence as they affect the perpetuation of living beings. Huxley begins by summing up the ground already covered.

In the last lecture, he reminds his hearers, he argued that living beings tend to reproduce their kind, yet also tend constantly to vary. Such variety might arise from causes we do not understand, and was therefore called spontaneous. It could appear as a definite, marked form, without gradations between itself and what came before. Once arisen, a variety might persist to a marked extent with no interference and no selection at work. That process, when exercised artificially by breeding, changes the picture. Huxley builds Darwin's case step by step, in plain speech meant for working listeners.
the-eventful-history-of-the-mutiny-and-p:
The Eventful History of the Mutiny and Piratical Seizure of H.M.S. Bounty, credited to Sir John Barrow, was printed at London in 1831. Its first chapter, Otaheite, heads the tale with Byron's lines on Tahiti's breadfruit groves, feasts without toil, and love unbought. Barrow then praises George the Third's reign for its sweep of new maps and sea lore.

Breadfruit, Bligh, and Christian's mutiny fill the famed tale. Barrow, an Admiralty man, used fresh papers to set the record. His book fixed the Bounty story in the public mind for a century.
the-first-hundred-thousand-being-the-uno:
Ian Hay, whose full name was Ian Hay Beith, wrote The First Hundred Thousand as the tale of a unit of Kitchener's first army. He served as a young officer in the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders.

The publishers' note says Beith joined up at the first outbreak of war in 1914, trained through the fall and winter at Aldershot, and reached the front in April. His unit was cut up in the September attack, and he rose to captain. The tale first ran, unsigned, in Blackwood's Magazine. With dry humor it shows raw town clerks and farm lads turned into soldiers.
the-hand-of-fu-manchu-being-a-new-phase-:
Sax Rohmer wrote The Hand of Fu-Manchu, described on its title page as a new phase in the activities of Fu-Manchu, the Devil Doctor. Chapter one, The Traveler from Tibet, opens in a room at the New Louvre Hotel in London. The narrator hears a strange sound in the corridor, part dragging and part tapping, and finds the passage thick with November fog.

Nothing moves when he looks, and the silence feels more like a desert than a city hotel. He blames his nerves after a hurried return from Cairo, then hears the sound again while he unpacks. Rohmer builds the threat slowly, through fog, stillness, and a noise that will not show its source.
the-history-of-henry-esmond-esq-a-colone:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The History of Henry Esmond, Esq., a colonel in the service of Her Majesty Queen Anne, written by himself. A dedication letter to Lord Ashburton, dated at London on October 18, 1852, asks leave to inscribe the volume for great kindness and friendship owed.

A preface, The Esmonds of Virginia, opens the family record. The estate of Castlewood in Virginia, in Westmoreland county between the Potomac and Rappahannock, was given to the family by King Charles the First for sacrifices in his cause. For near eighty years factors ran the plantations and grew rich, while the family received only a few scores of hogsheads of tobacco.
the-last-of-the-foresters-or-humors-on-t: John Esten Cooke published his story of the old Virginia frontier in 1856, naming himself as author of The Virginia Comedians and other tales. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing twenty-six chapters on Verty at Apple Orchard, Winchester, a schoolmaster named Roundjacket, and a necklace plot. The narrative itself, with Verty companions and border humor, does not appear in this record beyond those chapter titles.
the-letters-of-cassiodorus-being-a-conde:
Thomas Hodgkin published his condensed translation of the Variae letters of Cassiodorus at London in 1886. His preface says the abstract grew from close reading done while preparing volumes of his Italy and Her Invaders. Cassiodorus letters were his best, and often his only, source for parts of that history.

Cassiodorus served Gothic kings in Italy and wrote official letters in their names. Hodgkin shortens the full collection so historical students can use it with ease. Readers get court orders, appointments, and diplomacy from a Roman statesman keeping Roman forms alive under barbarian rule.
the-little-book-of-modern-verse-a-select: The Little Book of Modern Verse is an anthology of recent poetry edited by Jessie B. Rittenhouse. Only the opening header and title lines are present here, so none of the poems themselves appear. Those lines name the title and the editor, and identify the book as the first in a series of volumes associated with Rittenhouse. Nothing further about the selection, its poets, or its arrangement can be seen in what is present.
the-mano-bos-of-mindana-o-memoirs-of-the: John M. Garvan wrote The Manóbos of Mindanáo, issued as the first memoir of volume twenty-three of the Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences. The United States Government Printing Office published it in 1931, priced at one dollar in paper cover. Garvan presented it to the Academy at its annual meeting in 1929. Only the title pages and a transcriber's note are present here, so the text itself does not appear. The note explains that peso amounts are shown as P and centavo fractions converted to decimals.
the-meadow-brook-girls-in-the-hills-or-t: Janet Aldridge's The Meadow-Brook Girls in the Hills, subtitled The Missing Pilot of the White Mountains, was published by the Saalfield Publishing Company with a 1914 copyright. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The frontispiece introduces a guide named Janus Grubb. Chapter titles promise a man with green goggles, a night on a burning bridge, a slippery climb up high cliffs, and the tragedy of Chocorua.
the-mechanical-properties-of-wood-includ: Samuel J. Record, assistant professor of forest products at Yale University, published the first edition of The Mechanical Properties of Wood in 1914. Only the frontispiece note, title page, dedication, and a brief contents outline are present here, so the text itself does not appear. The frontispiece shows a photomicrograph of western hemlock, enlarged thirty-five times. Record dedicated the book to the staff of the Forest Products Laboratory at Madison, Wisconsin. His outline promises sections on cleavability, preservatives, and timber testing.
the-mysteries-of-free-masonry-containing:
Captain William Morgan's expose of Freemasonry was priced at one dollar. It is headed Morgan's Expose of Free Masonry. Only its title pages are present here, so the ritual degrees themselves do not appear. The full title promises all the degrees of the order conferred in a Master's Lodge, exactly as Morgan wrote them down.

A second title adds the degrees of the Royal Arch Chapter and the Grand Encampment of Knights Templars. Knights of the Red Cross, of the Christian Mark, and of the Holy Sepulchre are also named. A transcriber's note warns of inconsistent spelling in the original, corrected misprints, and footnotes moved to endnotes because the original has no chapters.
the-outdoor-girls-at-rainbow-lake-or-the:
Laura Lee Hope published The Outdoor Girls at Rainbow Lake in 1913, subtitled The Stirring Cruise of the Motor Boat Gem. The contents list twenty-five chapters, from A Grand Surprise to The Missing Saddle. Chapter One opens with Betty Nelson crossing a green lawn to squeeze into a hammock beside Grace Ford, promising her friends the grandest surprise.

The chapter titles map the cruise: missing documents, stowaways, a hint of ghosts, a regatta and a race, fighting fire, and a ghost caught at last. Hope, who also wrote the Bobbsey Twins books, gives her girls a motor boat, a lake camp, and a mystery to solve.
the-pocket-r-l-s-being-favourite-passage:
The Pocket R. L. S. collects favourite passages from the works of Robert Louis Stevenson, arranged as short readings divided by rows of stars. The first passage reflects that reading Stevenson leaves behind a memory of the man himself, as if a loyal hand had been touched and a noble friend made. A second passage turns to fame. It voices the wish to leave behind a portrait of the spirit rather than of the face.

Later passages treat the pleasure taken in beautiful nature as a capricious thing. It may fail for days in the very homeland of the beautiful. Then it can transfigure a place passed a thousand times, so the viewer sees it with a child's first pleasure, as Wordsworth saw the daffodils. Other lines picture women carrying burdens on their heads and sea-pines swept by wind.
the-pursuit-of-the-house-boat-being-some: John Kendrick Bangs published his sequel about the Associated Shades in 1897 with Harper and Brothers, illustrated by Peter Newell and dedicated to A. Conan Doyle with thanks for the detective's untimely death. Chapters begin with the shades taking action and a stranger unraveling a mystery, then organize a search party and hold conferences on deck and below stairs. Only the title pages, dedication, and opening of the contents list are present here, so the pursuit itself does not appear. The same contents appear in the companion 1919 record of the work.
the-scranton-high-chums-on-the-cinder-pa:
Donald Ferguson wrote The Scranton High Chums on the Cinder Path, or The Mystery of the Haunted Quarry. A Project Gutenberg note warns that this file has many errors. Readers are directed to a much cleaner version of the title. The contents promise twenty chapters. They move from five nut foragers through training for a great tournament. A mystery gathers around the old quarry road.

Later headings promise treachery in the air and a prowler caught in the act. Leon promises to reform. The crisis in Claude's life follows, with startling news from the Juggins boy. A searching party prowls around the quarry and meets a friendly ghost. The great marathon race fills the closing chapters. Chapter one opens on a Saturday afternoon in October. The bright sun is halfway down the western sky.
the-second-book-of-modern-verse-a-select: A Project Gutenberg header is the only matter preserved for The Second Book of Modern Verse. It names Jessie B. Rittenhouse as the book's editor. The e-text is numbered 1166 and dated January 1998. Alan R. Light prepared it, typing the original twice and comparing the copies electronically. The remaining pages are the project's standard notices about copyright, donations, and release dates. No poem, preface, contents list, or poet's name from the anthology itself appears here. The selection Rittenhouse made therefore cannot be described from these pages.
the-story-of-paul-boyton-voyages-on-all-: Paul Boyton's voyages appear here through title pages and contents alone. He paddled the world's great rivers, over twenty-five thousand miles in a rubber dress. The chapter summaries promise much adventure. A first attempt on the Allegheny leads off. Navy service and treasure diving follow. Wrecking and sharks come next. The life-saving service, African diamond fields, and the rubber dress itself appear too. Boyton appears before Queen Victoria, crosses the Channel, and descends the Rhine, Danube, and Mississippi. His narrative itself does not appear.
the-transgressors-story-of-a-great-sin-a: Francis A. Francis A. Adams, author of Who Rules America?, called The Transgressors a story of a great sin, and a political novel of the twentieth century. It was published at Philadelphia. This record gives a contents list in three books. Book one gathers clouds at Wilkes-Barre around Sheriff Trueman. Book two has the Syndicate incorporate, with a secret oath and a list of transgressors. Book three opens with a new party's birth. Adams's drama is mapped here, though its pages do not follow.
the-vaudois-teacher-and-other-poems-part:
John Greenleaf Whittier's narrative and legendary poems open the Standard Library Edition of his writings. A publishers' advertisement explains that Whittier himself rearranged and thoroughly revised the whole collection. He added head-notes giving the subject and occasion of certain poems, plus dates of first publication meant to fix when pieces were written.

Early poems discarded from earlier collections return in an appendix, at the publishers' request, making the edition complete and retrospective. Portraits prefixed to the volumes show successive periods of the poet's life. The contents for this part list The Vaudois Teacher, The Female Martyr, Pentucket, The Norsemen, Funeral Tree of the Sokokis, The Exiles, and other tales in verse.
the-young-wireless-operator-as-a-fire-pa: Lewis E. Theiss's The Young Wireless Operator — As a Fire Patrol, copyrighted in 1921, is shown through its dedication and opening contents. Theiss dedicates the story to Gifford Pinchot, the forestry leader. Pinchot's fight to save America's timber inspired the tale, he says. Chapters follow Charley into the mountains and a burned forest. A forest fire and an encounter with a bear are promised. The chapters themselves begin beyond the pages present here.
through-the-air-to-the-north-pole-or-the: Roy Rockwood wrote Through the Air to the North Pole, or the Wonderful Cruise of the Electric Monarch, in 1906. He also wrote The Rival Ocean Divers and A Schoolboy's Pluck. A contents list runs through seventeen chapters of airship adventure. Headings promise a runaway train, a strange rescuer, the airship itself, and a plan to seek the pole. Later chapters bring eagles, an ice cave, sea lions, a tornado, and captivity among Inuit. A contents list alone is on these pages, so Rockwood's story itself is not shown.
van-dyck-a-collection-of-fifteen-picture: Estelle M. Hurll wrote the introduction and readings for Van Dyck, in the Masterpieces of Art series. Houghton Mifflin issued the book in 1902. It holds fifteen pictures by the Flemish painter, plus a portrait of Van Dyck himself. That portrait, from the Prado Gallery at Madrid, serves as frontispiece. The pages given here hold the title page and contents only. The contents promise an essay on Van Dyck's character as an artist, a guide to books about him, and a directory of the pictures.
woman-s-institute-library-of-cookery-vol: Volume One of the Woman's Institute Library of Cookery covers basic cooking, cereals, bread, and hot breads. Pages present here hold a contents list, but no lessons or recipes. The list starts with food choice, food value, digestion, cooking methods, and kitchen tools. Cereal sections then cover corn, wheat, rice, oats, and Italian pastes. A breakfast menu closes the plan, judging by the contents alone.
wyandot-government-a-short-study-of-trib:
J. W. Powell wrote this short study of Wyandot tribal society for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology. He names four levels of organisation, running from the tribe down through the phratry and the gens to the family. The family means the household sharing one lodge or one section of a communal dwelling. A fire serves two families, one on each side. A woman heads each family, Powell notes.

The gens is a kin group traced through the female line. Each gens bears an animal name tied to a guardian spirit. Eleven gentes are listed, from Deer and Bear to Wolf and Sea Snake. Readers get a compact early account of Indigenous government.
